archetype.name: Super Bowl Contender (balanced)
archetype.definition: A team that ranks near the top of the league on both sides of the ball and backs its record with efficiency, not escapes: an explosive, efficient passing game paired with a defense that smothers the short game and the run.

report.headline: Last year's lucky 13-win team now plays like a true heavyweight.
report.take:
The 2025 Jaguars won 13 games while leading the league in wins over expected (3.87), the profile of a good team riding close games and bounces. The 2026 version has kept the record and earned it. Jacksonville is 7-2 with the league's best point differential per game (13.5) and the second-best net EPA (0.222). Its wins over expected has fallen to 0.85, so the record roughly matches how well it has played. This is a better team than the one that went 13-4, even if it may finish with fewer wins.

Trevor Lawrence has started every game, and the offense runs through his arm. Pass EPA per play is 0.247, third in the league, while the run game is a complement (rush EPA -0.037). Parker Washington is the clear WR1 by targets, with Jakobi Meyers and Brenton Strange behind him. Brian Thomas Jr. has a surprisingly small share, which says the timing game is working rather than the big-play outside receiver. On defense, the Jaguars are third in EPA allowed against both the pass and the run, first in EPA allowed on short passes, and first against opposing lead backs per play. Offenses that try to dink and run get nowhere.

The numbers hide two soft spots. The first is the deep ball: the defense ranks 28th in deep-pass EPA allowed, and Cincinnati threw for 428 yards and Houston for 312 in games Jacksonville barely won or lost. The pass rush pressures well (7th) but finishes poorly, with sacks ranked 23rd. The second is that the turnover margin, best in the league at 1.1 per game and +9 on the season, flatters the scoring margin. Short fields helped produce routs like 42-7 over Indianapolis. Some of that is skill, since they ranked third in turnover margin last year too, but takeaway rates swing, and the defense's points-allowed number will likely drift up toward its still-excellent EPA.

The trajectory is steep. After a September with a loss at Denver and two narrow wins, and a shootout loss to Houston, every game since the bye has been a comfortable win, capped by 352 passing yards and 16.2 pass EPA at Tennessee. With the rest of the AFC South well under .500, the division is close to a formality. The real tests are Chicago and Pittsburgh in the next month, which will show whether the deep-ball leak costs them against good offenses.

strengths.title: Efficient, explosive passing offense
strengths.body: Lawrence is running one of the league's most efficient passing games, third in pass EPA per play. The line keeps him reasonably clean, with sacks allowed ranked 5th. That protection matters because he holds the ball longer than most (time to throw 23rd). It has held up across opponents, from Philadelphia to Tennessee, and looks durable as long as the protection does.

strengths.title: Defense owns the underneath game
strengths.body: No defense in the league is stingier on short throws, and it ranks third in rush EPA allowed. Opposing lead backs produce the least per play against it of any defense. That forces offenses into low-percentage shots, which shows up in a top-4 red-zone defense. Because this rests on tackling and structure rather than turnovers, it is the most sustainable part of the profile.

strengths.title: Efficiency now matches the record
strengths.body: Last year's 13 wins came with the league's largest luck margin. This year the point differential and net EPA both rank at or near the top, and the record barely outruns the differential. Teams built this way tend to hold their level.

concerns.title: Deep passes beat this secondary
concerns.body: The flip side of squeezing the short game is a 28th-ranked deep-pass defense. Cincinnati and Houston, both top-10 offenses, threw for 300-plus against it. It is a structural cost of how the defense plays, and good quarterbacks in December will look for it.

concerns.title: Turnover margin inflates the scoreboard
concerns.body: A league-best turnover margin has turned good games into blowouts through short fields and extra possessions. A strong ranking last year suggests some of it is real ballhawking. Even so, the per-game rate is likely to cool, and points allowed will rise with it.

concerns.title: Pressure without finish, plus line penalties
concerns.body: The pass rush gets home often but rarely converts pressure into sacks. On the other side, the offensive line commits the sixth-most penalties per game. That produced a 125-yard penalty day at Cincinnati. Both are the kind of drive-level leaks that matter more against good teams than in routs.

trend.note: September was uneven: a loss at Denver, narrow wins over Cincinnati and Philadelphia, and a shootout loss to Houston. Every game since the Week 7 bye has been a decisive win, with the passing game peaking at Tennessee.

nextGame.headline: Lawrence gets the league's weakest pass rush, and a leaky red zone
nextGame.body:
The Giants are 5-3-1 under John Harbaugh, but their underlying numbers are middle of the pack: a 15th-ranked point differential and the second-highest wins over expected in the league. Their record leans on close wins. They play keep-away, second in time of possession, behind a run-first offense that ranks only 20th in rush EPA. That plays right into Jacksonville's top-3 run defense. The Giants defense is good between the 20s, fifth in yards allowed and first against deep passes. It also generates the least pressure in the league and allows touchdowns on 79% of red-zone trips, the worst rate in the league. The Book has Jacksonville a 6-point road favorite with a total of 46.5.

The main availability question is center Robert Hainsey, a 91% snap starter, who is questionable with a knee injury. Against the league's weakest pass rush, his absence is more likely to show up in snap-exchange and run-blocking details than in sacks. Rotational end Danny Striggow is in concussion evaluation. The Giants have cycled through three quarterbacks, with J.J. McCarthy starting the last three. Their only listed injuries are a part-time safety (Jason Pinnock, questionable) and a little-used linebacker who is out.

waysToWin.title: Cash in red-zone trips
waysToWin.body: The Giants turn red-zone stops into touchdowns allowed more often than anyone. A Jacksonville offense that sustains drives will get chances to score sevens instead of threes. That alone is likely enough to cover a modest Giants offense.

waysToWin.title: Clean pocket for the timing game
waysToWin.body: New York ranks last in pressure rate. That gives Lawrence, who holds the ball longer than most, time to work Washington, Meyers and Strange underneath and in the intermediate range. Avoiding the Giants' elite deep coverage costs little when the short game is this efficient.

waysToWin.title: Stuff the run, force McCarthy to pass
waysToWin.body: The Giants want to run, but Jacksonville is third in rush EPA allowed and first against lead backs. Once the Giants are behind schedule, a line that allows sacks at the 26th-ranked rate gives the Jaguars' pressure a chance to finally finish.

waysToLose.title: Giants shorten the game, win late
waysToLose.body: New York controls the clock as well as almost anyone and has thrived in one-score games. If it grinds out long drives and keeps the possession count low, a handful of plays decides it. Jacksonville has only split its one-score games.

waysToLose.title: Deep shots against a soft spot
waysToLose.body: Jacksonville's secondary ranks 28th against deep passes. One or two completed shots can flip a game the Giants otherwise lose on efficiency.

waysToLose.title: Penalties stall drives against a tight defense
waysToLose.body: The Giants rank first against deep passes, which blunts Jacksonville's big plays and forces long drives. A line that commits flags this often, possibly without its starting center, could kill those drives before they reach the red zone.

nextGame.watch: Whether Jacksonville's drives end in touchdowns: the league's worst red-zone defense against an offense that has been scoring 30-plus routinely.

restOfSeason.body:
The efficiency is real, so expect Jacksonville to keep winning most weeks. Points allowed should creep up as the league-best turnover margin cools and better offenses (Chicago, Pittsburgh, Dallas) test the deep-ball weakness. The division is effectively in hand, with every rival below .500 and two of the remaining games against Tennessee and Indianapolis. The open question is seeding, and the Chicago and Pittsburgh games in back-to-back weeks will decide whether this is a top-seed team or a very good wild-card-round host.

The pass offense looks sustainable given Lawrence's health and the protection. The run game will stay a complement, because backs get little room before contact (yards before contact ranks 30th) even though the line converts short yardage well. The blowout margins of late October and November will shrink, but the record should not suffer much.
swingFactors: Lawrence's health and the center position
Whether the deep secondary holds up against Chicago, Pittsburgh and Dallas
How fast the turnover margin regresses

confidence.note: Nine games of top-5 efficiency on both sides with a stable QB; turnover luck is the main source of noise.
